drills.q: Every deploy causes a brief burst of 502/connection-reset errors even though readiness probes look fine. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: No preStop hook (or one shorter than real Endpoints propagation time) means the container dies before endpoint removal has propagated to every kube-proxy, so some requests hit a pod that's already gone. Fix: add a preStop sleep tuned to worst-case propagation, ensure the app drains gracefully on SIGTERM, and make sure terminationGracePeriodSeconds exceeds preStop sleep plus drain time.

drills.q: A team says 'we have a PDB configured, so we're covered for availability during maintenance.' What's the gap in that claim?
drills.a: A PDB only paces voluntary disruptions (drains, upgrades, autoscaler consolidation) via the Eviction API — it provides zero protection against involuntary disruptions like node crashes, OOMKilled pods, CrashLoopBackOff, or an HPA/Deployment scaling down replicas directly. It also doesn't guarantee the surviving replicas are actually healthy.

drills.q: A routine node upgrade hangs indefinitely on one namespace's pods. The PDB looks correctly configured. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: The PDB's minAvailable is set equal to (or too close to) the Deployment's actual current replica count, so no eviction can ever succeed without violating the budget. Check whether replica count shrank over time (deliberate scale-down or HPA) while the PDB stayed static, creating this deadlock.

drills.q: A slow-starting JVM service keeps getting killed and restarted during its first two minutes of startup, even though it eventually becomes healthy. What's missing?
drills.a: A startupProbe. Without it, liveness has to either use a short initialDelaySeconds (kills the app before it finishes starting) or a long one (which then also delays catching genuinely hung processes during steady state). startupProbe decouples the two, gating liveness/readiness until startup succeeds once.

drills.q: A pod creation is rejected with a quota-exceeded error even though the namespace's ResourceQuota shows plenty of CPU/memory headroom. Why might that be?
drills.a: ResourceQuota can also cap object counts (count/pods, count/persistentvolumeclaims), not just compute resources — the namespace may have hit its pod-count or PVC-count ceiling, a separate dimension from the compute numbers usually checked first.

drills.q: A cluster's cloud bill has tripled year over year with no corresponding traffic growth. A colleague proposes buying more reserved instances. What should you check first, and why?
drills.a: The gap between requested and actually-used capacity per namespace/workload via Kubecost/OpenCost attribution. Unoptimized clusters commonly run at only 10-30% actual CPU utilization against requested capacity — buying reserved capacity locks in a discount on that same waste instead of fixing it; rightsize requests first, then commit capacity against the corrected baseline.

drills.q: A team claims they 'do canary deployments with Kubernetes' using a plain Deployment. How do you probe whether this is a genuine traffic-weighted canary or just a rolling update with a different name?
drills.a: Ask specifically what decides to proceed or roll back, and on what signal. A genuine canary system references specific metrics/analysis templates and traffic percentages (Argo Rollouts, Flagger). If the answer is really 'we deploy a few pods first and watch dashboards manually,' that's an informal rolling update, not automated progressive delivery — Deployment's RollingUpdate has no native traffic-percentage or metric-gated logic.

drills.q: A multi-tenant cluster has ResourceQuota, LimitRange, and NetworkPolicy applied per namespace, yet one tenant's batch job is still degrading another tenant's latency-critical service. What isolation gap does this expose?
drills.a: Namespace-level controls (quota, limit range, network policy) don't provide physical isolation — tenants still share a kernel, node network stack, and scheduler. Noisy-neighbor CPU/node contention can cross tenant boundaries even with all three controls correctly applied. The fix is dedicated node pools (taints/tolerations) or separate clusters for tenants needing stronger isolation.
